articles.title: She lost $600,000 in a pig-butchering scam. Then came the tax bill
articles.summary: Lori Flowers forked over $600,000 to scammers in a pig-butchering scheme, drawing much of the money from her 401(k). Then came the tax bill.
articles.body:
When the man from Brussels asked Lori Flowers to lend him $400,000 from her 401(k), she thought she was bailing out her best friend.

By the time the "pig-butchering" scam was over, Flowers had forked over $600,000, funds she would never see again.

American tax law used to protect victims of theft such as Flowers – until Congress gutted the provision when it passed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act in 2017.

Still reeling from the 2022 theft, Flowers learned she owed another $225,000 in taxes and penalties on money she had withdrawn from her retirement account for the scammers. The IRS treated it as income. Flowers declared bankruptcy.

"This is my credit," she said. "This is my livelihood."

Now, a bill in Congress would restore legal protections for scam victims like Flowers, lifting the burden of paying taxes on stolen funds.

The Tax Relief for Fraud Victims Act won House approval on Sept. 15. It awaits action in the Senate.

"I think it has strong bipartisan support," said Chuck Bell , programs director for advocacy at Consumer Reports. "I think no one wants to defend this awful provision of the tax code."

Did Congress inadvertently strip away tax protections for scam victims?

Congress stripped away the tax deduction for theft victims in 2017, then did it again in 2025, making a temporary measure permanent.

Most lawmakers apparently didn't grasp the real-world significance of the law change until recently, when victims like Flowers came forward.

"You get scammed, and then the IRS comes after you," said Clark Flynt-Barr, government affairs director for financial security at AARP. "You have no money, and now you're going to owe more money."

When Flynt-Barr explains current law to members of Congress, she said, "They're typically pretty shocked: 'What do you mean, we're taxing people on money that was stolen from them?'"

The "casualty and theft loss" deduction was one of many items Congress and President Donald Trump cut from the tax code in 2017 as they introduced a higher standard deduction.

"I haven't been able to find reasoning other than, 'We were trying to clean up the tax code," Flynt-Barr said.

And why did it take nearly a decade for Congress to make it right?

One reason, Flynt-Barr and others said, is that scam victims often hide their victimhood even from loved ones and closest friends, out of shame.

In 2025, Americans age 60 and over reported $7.7 billion in losses to fraud, according to AARP, citing federal data. But the true figure might be closer to $80 billion, because of under-reporting.

articles.title: EPA launches drinking water study looking for traces of abortion pills
articles.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is launching a drinking water quality study that will for the first time look for traces of abortion pills mifepristone and misoprostol — something anti-abortion activists, attorneys general and lawmakers have been lobbying the agency to do for years. The agency stopped short of making mifepristone an official water contaminant…
articles.body:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is launching a drinking water quality study that will for the first time look for traces of abortion pills mifepristone and misoprostol — something anti-abortion activists, attorneys general and lawmakers have been lobbying the agency to do for years.

The agency stopped short of making mifepristone an official water contaminant that would require regulation, but abortion opponents are hopeful the move is a precursor to restricting access to the drug, or at a minimum influencing a debate about its safety.

“It is exciting after a very long journey that’s been almost 10 years, to have this be taken seriously enough to be on an official list,” Kristi Hamrick, head of policy at Students for Life of America (SFLA), said in an interview. “But that doesn’t change the fact that there’s a lot of information that we need, for it to be useful for people to know.”

EPA earlier this month announced it will be conducting a “cutting edge scientific study” that will test for “emerging” contaminants. The agency will pick several locations in metropolitan areas across the country and screen for more than 1,400 pharmaceuticals, pesticides and other chemicals, including mifepristone and misoprostol.

EPA is also planning to screen for hormones such as testosterone and progesterone, as well as medications like levonorgestrel, which is used in some contraceptives and the morning-after pill.

There is no evidence that abortion pills are harming the water supply or are harmful to people. Environmental scientists and abortion rights advocates dismissed EPA’s effort as a political stunt from the Trump administration aimed at placating an increasingly frustrated anti-abortion movement ahead of the midterm elections.

Anna Bernstein, principal federal policy adviser for the Guttmacher Institute, said she isn’t necessarily worried that the Trump administration will take immediate concrete action to restrict mifepristone based off the study results. Instead, Bernstein said, state and local officials could use it as justification for crackdowns.

“I think what’s concerning here is that there’s already a culture of criminalization around abortion, especially since Dobbs [v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization], and the potential to use this as justification for further surveillance could create more fear for abortion seekers, for providers at a time when folks are already being criminalized and for their pregnancy outcomes, including abortion,” Bernstein said.

Nathan Donley, the environmental health science director at the Center for Biological Diversity, said there are chemicals on EPA’s list that are known contaminants and that should be regulated. But mifepristone is not one of them.

“There are major water contaminants that need to be regulated, and testing for those things can be good as long as regulation happens. And then on the other hand, if we’re wasting time on a witch hunt for … those things like mifepristone, then that’s time and resources we take away from regulating and studying things that that are actually a problem,” Donley said.

Donley noted that by comparison, other pharmaceuticals taken daily by tens of millions of Americans enter wastewater systems in far greater quantities without any evidence of harm.

“Its presence on the list is meant to stigmatize the drug instead of a true effort to try and identify a new water contaminant,” Donley said.

EPA’s tests will only show whether a chemical is present in the water, not how much of it or whether there is any harm to humans. It’s not clear yet where EPA will conduct the tests, or what it will do with the results.

“EPA is currently working with the water sector to identify water systems to participate in the study,” the agency said in a statement to The Hill. “EPA expects the study to take place over the next year. EPA is committed to transparency and will publish results via reports and peer-reviewed literature after data analysis and all quality assurance reviews are completed.”

The testing campaign is not part of the agency’s routine update to the Safe Drinking Water Act’s contaminant list, or any other established unregulated contaminant monitoring lists, so there is no regulation required.

The unregulated contaminants list is a way for EPA to collect nationwide data on chemicals, which could be used to set federal limits in the future.

But scientists said any process that could set limits on mifepristone in drinking water would take years. Instead, they expect the study results will be used as part of the broader campaign to get mifepristone pulled from the market.

“This is kind of end-running the whole Safe Drinking Water Act required monitoring program, and going directly to an unprecedented fishing expedition,” said Betsy Southerland, a former career scientist in EPA’s Office of Water who left during the first Trump administration.

“I don’t think in any stretch of the imagination [EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin] is planning for this 10-year process to take place to put a drinking water standard out for mifepristone. I think he’s planning to use the immediate results to try to get FDA [Food and Drug Administration] to take it off the market,” Southerland said.

Medication has become the most common method of abortion since Roe v. Wade was overturned, and limiting the availability of the pills — which women usually take at home in the first 10 weeks of pregnancy — has become a major focus of the antiabortion movement.

SFLA has been the primary organization on the front line of pushing EPA to investigate how mifepristone might be contaminating the water supply, and to require utilities nationwide to monitor for the drugs.

The organization alleges more than 50 tons of medical waste are flushed into water systems each year as a result of abortion drugs, causing significant environmental harm.

“There are no studies finding mifepristone in the water. It’s because those studies haven’t been done, and the reason those studies haven’t been done is because we use so little of this compared to other bona fide water contaminants, and it doesn’t have the chemical hallmarks of known water contaminants,” said Donley.

Kristan Hawkins, SFLA’s president, in a statement said EPA’s study was “an exciting first step,” but noted that the group is still pushing for “mandated, ongoing testing.”

In announcing the study, EPA did not mention either of the two abortion pills. Instead, it tied the action to the Make America Healthy Again Movement, led by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

“We have heard loud and clear that Americans are concerned about potential unknown pollutants lurking in their drinking water,” Zeldin said in a statement. “What we learn will provide clarity and peace of mind while guiding the agency’s continued efforts to Make America Healthy Again.”

articles.title: Tariffs, fuel costs, and rising rates squeeze U.S. manufacturers
articles.summary: A three-way squeeze on American businesses is forcing price increases, inventory hoarding, and in some cases bankruptcy filings
articles.body:
American businesses across manufacturing, transportation, and retail are being hit from three directions at once: tariffs that have raised the cost of raw materials, record fuel prices driven by the war with Iran, and the Federal Reserve's first interest rate increase in three years, according to CNBC .

Allen Eden, the 56-year-old owner of the Original Saw Co., a 25-person industrial power saw maker in Britt, Iowa, told CNBC that uncertainty over future parts availability has led him to build up larger reserves of inventory than he would ordinarily keep on hand. A single bracket his motors depend on went from $42 to $87 over the summer — a price increase of more than 100 percent. Price increases for his saws, sold to retailers including Home Depot and directly to manufacturers, look inevitable, he said.

Middle-market manufacturers are caught in a particularly tight bind. Rising steel and aluminum costs push them to raise prices, feeding inflation — and the Fed's rate hike then makes it more expensive to finance the inventory and equipment they need to keep running. Because smaller companies tend to carry short-duration debt, Fed rate moves translate into higher borrowing costs with little delay, JPMorgan Chase global strategy head Dubravko Lakos-Bujas wrote in a September 14 note cited by CNBC.

"The combination of higher rates and higher fuel prices means that sectors with heavy exposure to both are first in the line of fire," Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon, told CNBC.

Auto suppliers illustrate the pressure. Lucerne International, a Detroit-area auto parts manufacturer operating as a private company, suspended its U.S. production and scrapped a planned $50 million aluminum forging facility in Michigan. CEO Mary Buchzeiger cited higher costs for raw materials and finished parts tied to what she called "Trump tariffs 2.0." The company has shifted its U.S. operations to warehousing, distribution, and tariff-mitigation services, which she said carry better margins.

Grupo Antolin, a Spanish auto parts maker that counts Ford, GM, Volkswagen, and Stellantis among its customers, sought Chapter 15 bankruptcy protection in the U.S. in July, with tariffs, rising raw-material and energy costs, and supply-chain disruptions cited as causes.

Diesel prices are a major driver of the squeeze. As diesel's national average climbed to an unprecedented $6.27 a gallon , the war with Iran has restricted tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz while Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refining infrastructure prompted Moscow to ban diesel exports — together removing roughly 20% of the diesel that normally moves by sea, according to analysts at ING.

articles.title: Trump: Russia has ‘lost control’ of diesel industry because of Ukraine war
articles.summary: President Trump on Monday acknowledged major Ukrainian military strikes have hit Russian energy infrastructure hard, saying Russia has lost control of its diesel oil industry and calling for an end to the war. “A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission,” Trump wrote in…
articles.body:
President Trump on Monday acknowledged major Ukrainian military strikes have hit Russian energy infrastructure hard, saying Russia has lost control of its diesel oil industry and calling for an end to the war.

“A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social following a call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday.

Trump said “Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine” and called for the war to end.

“This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended. The whole World suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!”

The post came after Ukraine launched a massive drone strike against Russia overnight between Saturday and Sunday. More than 1,600 drones traveled nearly 280 miles into the country, striking oil refineries in Moscow, causing fires and triggering a pause in operations, according to an analysis by the Institute for the Study of War.

Zelensky, in a post on the social platform X, said Russia launched attacks Monday on Zaporizhzhia in the southeast, hitting residential buildings, a university facility, shopping mall and boiler house, with five people injured. A separate drone attack in the northeast city of Kharkiv killed one woman, Zelensky said.

“Russia is not backing down from its escalation and is sending many signals that it is ready to expand the war,” Zelensky said.

Trump has revived efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine even as the U.S. remains engaged in its war with Iran, the major consequences being disruption to global energy exports with the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz and threats to shipping in the Red Sea following a lightning offensive by the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.

Oil prices have risen as a result of the fighting, with diesel prices in the United States in particular skyrocketing.

The national average price for diesel has reached $6.27 per gallon, largely as a result of the ongoing U.S. war in Iran, though Trump has sought to cast blame on energy facilities hit as part of the Russia-Ukraine war.

The higher diesel prices are a big political problem for Trump and the GOP, with Republican senators saying it is a challenge in several competitive races.

Earlier this month, Trump dispatched his top envoys for negotiations, Steve Witkoff, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv for talks on ending the war.

Zelensky, in a post on X, thanked Trump for sending Kushner and Witkoff to Kyiv and said that the president agreed to meet with him on the sidelines of the U.N. summit this week. Zelensky said “the peace track is our number one priority.”

“There are ideas for de-escalation steps and for addressing fundamental security issues – energy security, food security, and the protection of human life. We are working together with the American team and are ready to take really serious steps,” Zelensky said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio may meet with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the U.N. summit, Ukrainian media reported , citing Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova.

articles.title: Bessent: US suggesting AI alert system with China ahead of Trump-Xi talks

The system, called the “U.S.-China AI dialogue,” would create a mechanism for the two superpowers to communicate when there are incidents that rise to “a national security…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday the U.S. is proposing a notification system between Washington and Beijing on AI amid growing concerns about the technology’s risks to humanity.

The system, called the “U.S.-China AI dialogue,” would create a mechanism for the two superpowers to communicate when there are incidents that rise to “a national security level from AI,” Bessent explained to reporters.

“We think that just like with any cross-border activity that moving from opaque to more transparency between the No. 1 and No. 2 AI powers in the world is very important,” he said after meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.

Bessent and his Chinese counterpart convened in New York ahead of President Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

This comes at a moment when conversations about AI safety have reached a fever pitch in Washington, after several researchers offered dire warnings about AI’s potential to destroy humanity.

Several American AI leaders have called for a slowdown in the technology’s development. But Trump has so far resisted a push for the federal government to institute guardrails, frequently pointing to the need to stay ahead of China.

The fierce competition between the two countries makes coordination on the issue difficult. The U.S. has long imposed strict export controls on the flow of advanced AI chips to China in an effort to stymie Beijing’s efforts at development.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer noted Sunday that export controls “were not on the agenda.”

articles.title: Houthis say US ships won’t be targeted in Red Sea
articles.summary: The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have reportedly reassured the Trump administration that they won’t attack U.S. ships in the Red Sea. Senior Houthi official Mohamed al-Bukhaiti told The Associated Press that the administration reached out to his group earlier this month after Houthis took several towns and islands along Yemen’s western coast, which are crucial to…
articles.body:
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have reportedly reassured the Trump administration that they won’t attack U.S. ships in the Red Sea.

Senior Houthi official Mohamed al-Bukhaiti told The Associated Press that the administration reached out to his group earlier this month after Houthis took several towns and islands along Yemen’s western coast, which are crucial to controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

“We confirmed that we are not targeting the United States, or any other nation, in the strait, with the sole exception of the Saudi enemy,” al-Bukhaiti told the AP. “That remains the case.”

President Trump has reportedly rebuffed several requests from Saudi Arabia to launch strikes on the Houthis, with the most recent plea coming Thursday from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

The New York Times reported that the president was prepared to launch airstrikes against the Houthis after speaking with the crown prince, but on Sunday he reversed course.

Washington has instead sent advisers to support the kingdom, which has had its key energy pipelines attacked recently and its capital targeted by a ballistic missile over the weekend.

Trump previously took a harder approach to the Houthis, ordering strikes on the group in March 2025 in response to attacks on shipping vessels in the Red Sea. Those plans were famously shared by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on a Signal chat that included The Atlantic’s editor in chief.

However, the administration is reluctant to become involved with the Houthis this time around, as it is focused on its war in Iran, fighting that has depleted advanced munitions stockpiles and threatened to spill into a wider regional conflict.

articles.body:
Major cryptocurrency super PAC Fairshake plans to spend $30 million in Ohio opposing former Sen. Sherrod Brown’s (D) bid to return to the Senate, the group confirmed to The Hill.

Brown, who spent nearly two decades representing the Buckeye State before being ousted in 2024, is facing off against incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R) in a tight midterm race that could be crucial to determining partisan control of the upper chamber.

The crypto industry spent heavily against Brown two years ago, pouring about $40 million into the race and helping to elect Sen. Bernie Moreno (R), a crypto enthusiast. Brown, who previously chaired the Senate Banking Committee, had taken a more skeptical approach toward digital assets.

Fairshake still has a hefty finance account at its disposal with just six weeks left until the midterms. It reported $108 million on hand at the end of August.

The super PAC’s latest spending comes after a major crypto regulation bill fell short in the Senate. The Clarity Act, which has long been a key priority for the industry, failed to clear a procedural hurdle on the Senate floor last week, with every Democrat and several Republicans blocking the measure.

Many in the industry and in Congress suggested the legislation was dead following the failed vote. The Clarity Act’s supporters had hoped to get the bill across the finish line before the midterms, which could change control of one or both chambers and reduce incentives to pass the current measure.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will give remarks Monday as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) rolls out a new artificial intelligence tool aimed at helping air traffic controllers manage congestion and reduce flight delays.

The Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories (SMART) program will use AI to analyze air travel, airport capacity and weather. The rollout will begin at Reagan Washington National, Dulles International and Baltimore-Washington International airports, according to the Transportation Department.

Duffy earlier this year brushed off concerns that AI would replace the controllers. Risks of the rapidly evolving technology have captured headlines in recent weeks.

The press conference is scheduled to begin at 12:30 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: His home changed hands for $5. Could it happen to your family?
articles.summary: A South Carolina caregiver allegedly gained power of attorney over a 75-year-old with Parkinson's, then transferred his home via quitclaim deed for $5.
articles.body: A deed can change hands without a burglar breaking a window or a scammer hacking a computer. Sometimes the first warning signs are sitting inside county records, bank accounts and email inboxes, waiting for someone to notice. A disturbing case out of South Carolina shows why families may want to put a few digital safeguards in place now. According to a local report, a daughter says her 75-year-old father, who had Parkinson's disease and a brain injury, became increasingly isolated after a caregiver entered his life. Within weeks, the caregiver was named as his power of attorney. A quitclaim deed later transferred his Conway home to her for $5. His daughter also says bank statements show money moving from his account to the caregiver, including after his death. Conway police said they were investigating. The allegations have not been proven in court. Still, the case raises a question every family with an aging or vulnerable loved one should consider: Would you know if someone changed a deed, moved money or took control of an important account? Technology cannot prevent every form of financial exploitation. However, the right alerts can create an early-warning system that makes major changes much harder to hide. No technical experience is needed. Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com MAN ACCUSED OF STEALING MORE THAN $735K AS POWER OF ATTORNEY TO PURCHASE PROPERTY, ONLYFANS AND LIFE COACHING Why this case goes beyond home-title theft Home-title theft usually involves a criminal forging documents, impersonating an owner or recording a fraudulent deed. The allegations in this case raise a different concern. The daughter alleges that her father was vulnerable and may not have understood what he signed after the caregiver obtained power of attorney. A forged deed can involve identity theft. When someone signs a document after alleged manipulation or coercion or when questions arise about whether that person understood what they were signing, the legal issues can involve undue influence, elder financial exploitation or abuse of legal authority. Technology cannot determine what happened between two people. What it can do is flag events that deserve a closer look, including a new deed filing, an ownership change, a new lender, an unusual bank transfer or a change to an account's contact information. The FBI has warned that quitclaim deed fraud can involve forged documents as well as relatives or close associates persuading older adults to transfer property for someone else's financial gain. The agency recommends monitoring property records and enrolling in county title alerts where available. 5 digital safeguards that can help protect your family You do not need expensive technology to start watching for suspicious changes. Some of the strongest safeguards are free alerts already offered by county governments, banks and financial institutions. The key is setting them up before something happens and making sure the warnings reach someone who can act. Here are five digital safeguards worth putting in place. DIY IDENTITY PROTECTION VS PAID SERVICES: WHAT WORKS IN 2026 1) Sign up for free county property alerts Start with the government office that records deeds in the county where the property is located. Depending on the state, it may be called the county recorder, recorder of deeds, register of deeds or clerk's office. Many of these offices offer a free notification service. Look for names such as Property Fraud Alert, Recording Notification Service, Fraud Guard or Land Record Alert. Horry County, where the South Carolina property is located, now offers a free Recording Notification Service. It monitors the county's registry for new filings associated with a registered name and sends an alert when it finds one. To find a service in your area: Keep in mind that an alert does not stop a document from being recorded. Instead, it tells you something was filed so you can investigate quickly. 2) Turn on detailed bank and credit alerts The reported deed transfer was only one warning sign in this case. The daughter also alleges that money moved from her father's bank account. Most banks and credit card issuers let you create alerts through their apps or websites. You will usually find them under Settings , Security , Alerts or Notifications . Turn on alerts for withdrawals and outgoing transfers, new external accounts or payees, large purchases, checks clearing, low balances, password resets, new device logins and changes to contact information. Also consider setting transaction alerts at a relatively low dollar amount. Scammers sometimes begin with smaller transactions before trying to move more money. Whenever possible, use more than one notification method, such as push notifications, text messages and email. Then review those settings every few months. A new phone, changed email address or bank app update can sometimes interrupt notifications. 3) Add a trusted contact without giving up control A trusted contact gives a financial institution another person to reach if it sees signs of exploitation or cannot contact the account holder. That person does not automatically become a joint owner and does not receive power of attorney simply because they were named as a trusted contact. For brokerage accounts, FINRA rules require firms to make a reasonable effort to obtain a trusted contact. The contact may be asked about the account holder's health, current contact information or possible financial exploitation. Being named a trusted contact does not give someone permission to trade, withdraw money or view account balances. Some banks and credit unions offer similar protections voluntarily. Ask the fraud department or elder financial exploitation team whether it provides trusted contacts, read-only account access, extra confirmation for large transfers or additional review when money goes to a new recipient. Choose the person carefully. If a daily caregiver already has access to finances, consider using a different relative, attorney or accountant as the trusted contact. That creates another set of eyes without handing over control of the account. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says trusted contacts can help financial institutions respond to possible elder financial exploitation while allowing the account holder to retain control. 4) Protect the phone and email receiving the alerts Alerts only help when they reach the right person. If someone else controls the account holder's phone or email, they may be able to delete warnings, change contact information or reset passwords before a family member notices. Start with the email account connected to banking, investment and property notifications. Use a password manager to create and store a strong, unique password. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). Review recovery phone numbers and email addresses. Check for unfamiliar forwarding rules and signed-in devices. Store backup codes somewhere secure that the person legally authorized to use the account can reach. Then protect the mobile carrier account too. Add an account PIN and enable any protection the carrier offers against unauthorized number transfers. Someone who takes over a phone number may be able to intercept security codes and account alerts. Also, avoid sharing one online banking password among several relatives or caregivers. Instead, ask the financial institution about separate authorized access, a view-only login or another supported arrangement. Separate logins make it much easier to see who accessed or changed an account. 5) Add broader monitoring for property and financial activity County and bank alerts provide a strong foundation, but they live in different places. A broader identity theft protection service can bring more warning signs together and provide help if identity theft becomes complicated. Some services offer home title monitoring that looks for changes involving property ownership, new lenders, financing and notices of default. Depending on the provider and plan, you may also get alerts for suspicious activity involving checking, savings, credit, retirement and investment accounts. In a situation like the South Carolina case, a recorded ownership change could potentially trigger an alert. Suspicious financial activity may also surface when affected accounts are connected and the activity meets the service's monitoring criteria. Some identity theft protection plans also provide access to restoration specialists who can help if identity theft or home-title fraud occurs. However, monitoring has limits. Home title monitoring relies on county records, and newly recorded documents can sometimes take time to appear in monitoring systems. These services cannot block a deed, determine whether someone understood a document or prevent someone from misusing power of attorney. Coverage, reimbursement and insurance benefits vary by provider and plan and may come with terms, conditions and exclusions. A dispute involving alleged coercion or a deed that someone actually signed may also be handled differently from a case involving forged identity theft. Think of monitoring as an alarm, not a lock. It can warn you that something changed so you can investigate. It cannot make the change impossible. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com Why a credit freeze will not stop a deed transfer A credit freeze remains one of the best tools for making it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts in someone's name. However, freezing your credit does not lock a property title. It also cannot stop activity inside an existing bank account or prevent someone from filing a deed. Use a credit freeze alongside property alerts, financial monitoring and secure account logins. Warning signs families should watch for Digital alerts can flag transactions and account changes, but families should also pay attention to changes in behavior and access. Take a closer look if an older or vulnerable person suddenly stops communicating with family, becomes unusually isolated or has a new caregiver or acquaintance speaking for them. Other warning signs include unexplained financial or legal decisions, missing bank statements or tax bills, unfamiliar people appearing on accounts, sudden password or address changes and property documents signed for little or no apparent value. One change may have a perfectly reasonable explanation. Several changes appearing around the same time deserve attention. What to do if you suspect exploitation If something feels wrong, move quickly while preserving records that could help investigators understand what happened. The CFPB says family members do not need every detail before reporting suspected elder financial abuse. Investigators can determine what happened. THE SCAM TEXT TEST: SPOT DANGER BEFORE YOU TAP Kurt's key takeaways The most unsettling part of this case goes beyond a home allegedly changing hands for $5. It is how many major changes may have happened before the family knew what was going on. No app can tell you whether a vulnerable loved one is being manipulated. A title-monitoring service also cannot replace regular conversations, careful legal planning and people you trust. Technology can still give families an important advantage: an earlier warning. Set up county property alerts. Turn on detailed financial notifications. Add a trusted contact. Secure the phone and email accounts receiving those alerts. Then consider broader monitoring if your family wants another layer of visibility across property, identity and financial accounts. The sooner you know something changed, the sooner you can start asking questions and take action. Have you set up property or financial alerts for yourself or an aging family member? articles.body:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) said in a new interview that he has dropped 80 pounds using a GLP-1 drug.

“I have been driven my whole life to lose weight,” Pritzker said in an interview that aired Monday on “CBS Mornings.”

“The fact that I am now able to do it because this GLP-1 became available is truly, like, I mean, it’s something that has meant a lot to me,” he added.

Medicines including semaglutide , tirzepatide and dulaglutide, which are commercially marketed as Ozempic, Mounjaro and Trulicity respectively, are GLP-1 drugs. They function by mimicking a hormone made by the human body that stimulates insulin secretion and reduces appetite.

A survey from Gallup in July found a record number of Americans taking GLP-1 drugs for weight loss. In the poll, 11 percent of Americans were using a GLP-1 medication to lose weight, an 8-point jump from 2024.

President Trump, who has faced comments about his own weight, has a history of scrutinizing the Illinois governor’s body.

In late August 2025, Pritzker said personal attacks from the president “are just evidence of a guy who’s still living in fifth grade,” following Trump criticizing the governor’s appearance.

“It takes one to know one, on the weight question,” Pritzker said at the time. “And the president, of course, himself, is not in good shape. So, he ought to respond to that from me.”

The president has previously said that the Illinois governor “ought to spend more time in the gym, actually” and accused Pritzker of being “too busy eating” to lead his state.

articles.title: Some iPhone users may get up to $95 in settlement over Siri claims: How to apply
articles.summary: The claim process has opened for a massive settlement involving select iPhones.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – If you own one of several newer iPhone models, you may now be eligible to submit a claim in a $250 million settlement over Apple’s AI system.

Earlier this year, Apple agreed to settle a lawsuit that accused its Siri Apple Intelligence features of failing to meet expectations. Consumers alleged Apple misled them about the capabilities of Apple Intelligence when it unveiled it in 2024, and, when the iPhone 16 came out later that year, users said several teased features were not immediately available.

Apple has denied any wrongdoing in this settlement.

“Since the launch of Apple Intelligence, we have introduced dozens of features across many languages that are integrated across Apple’s platforms, relevant to what users do every day, and built with privacy protections at every step,” a spokesperson for Apple said in a statement shared with Nexstar earlier this year. “These include Visual Intelligence, Live Translation, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Clean Up and many more.”

“Apple has reached a settlement to resolve claims related to the availability of two additional features. We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users.”

The claim window for the settlement, which could pay out up to $95 per device, is opening Monday, according to settlement administrators.

Some 37 million devices bought in the U.S. between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, are covered in the settlement. All iPhone 16 models and the iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max are among those covered devices. ( Apple Intelligence features are only available on iPhone 16 and 17 models and the iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max. iPhone 17 models, however, were not yet available within the aforementioned settlement window.)

If you bought a qualifying iPhone 15 or 16 model within that timeframe, you may qualify for $25 per device. That amount could go up to $95, depending on how many claims are filed, “and other factors,” court filings said.

Qualifying class members are expected to be notified via email about the settlement. That email will have a claim ID and PIN used to complete a claim form , though an option does exist for those who believe they qualify and did not receive a claim ID and PIN.

You’ll be able to file a claim online at smartphoneaisettlement.com , which is available to individuals, businesses, and entities who purchased a qualifying iPhone model in the necessary timeframe.

Administrators say you may need your device’s serial number, which can be found in Settings, then General, and then About. A claim form can be completed for each qualifying device you own.

When filing a claim, you’ll be able to select from one of four payment options: paper check, PayPal, Venmo, or a digital check.

It’s not clear when exactly payments will be sent out. Settlement administrators say an approval hearing is scheduled for Feb. 24, 2027, though that date could move. Appeals may also delay the payout process.

“If there is no appeal, your settlement benefit will be processed promptly,” administrators say online.

You have until Dec. 21, 2026, to exclude yourself from, object to, or file a claim for the settlement.

Apple Intelligence is among the several features that Apple made improvements to in its latest iOS update, 27 , which was released earlier this month. That includes “new Siri AI,” with its own app, according to Apple . Siri will be “an even more capable AI assistant with expanded intelligence to be more helpful every day” as part of the update.

You’ll find new AI editing tools for your photos, too, and will be able to use your Camera to perform a visual search, with Siri’s help. ( A similar feature already exists. ) While on a call, “Call Context” will find “relevant information from across your apps,” like a flight confirmation code while calling an airline, Apple explains.

articles.title: Exclusive-Fed's Musalem says more rate hikes likely needed to quell inflation
articles.summary: By Howard Schneider WASHINGTON, Sept 21 (Reuters) - The Federal Reserve will likely need to hike interest rates further to lower inflation resulting from str...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Sept 21 (Reuters) - The Federal Reserve will likely need to hike interest rates further to lower inflation resulting from strong demand as well as a commodity price shock that has moved beyond oil, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said on Monday, adding that it would be better for the US central bank ‌to act sooner than wait.

"Both persistent demand and recurring supply forces are continuing to contribute to keeping inflation risks elevated, and I judge that without further policy restraint on ‌inflation it is more likely to be substantially above our 2% target in 18 months than at target," Musalem said in an interview with Reuters.

"I think it's crucial that policy puts a meaningful restraint on inflation" so the Fed reaches its ​inflation target in about a year and a half, allowing time for tighter policy to impact the economy, he said.

Musalem, who is not currently a voting member of the central bank's rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee, would not comment on the Fed's possible next steps or the estimated level the policy rate may need to reach to lower inflation.

But "earlier and incremental policy firming is better and less disruptive than later and larger and potentially more abrupt policy action" further in the future, he said.

Inflation "is not a risk. It's there," Musalem said, noting that even after stripping out the impact of oil and other supply-related factors, underlying inflation ‌is running perhaps a percentage point above the Fed's target and is "moving ⁠in the wrong direction."

Little progress has been made recently in the battle to bring inflation back down to the 2% target. The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, the Fed's main inflation gauge, was at 3.7% on a year-over-year basis in July, compared to a recent low of 2.3% in April of 2025, ⁠as the Trump administration rolled out its plan for global import tariffs.

The shock to import prices was followed this year by the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which pushed up fuel costs globally, with the price of diesel hitting a record high recently. Prices for commodities like copper have also been rising, Musalem said, as an offshoot of the artificial intelligence investment boom.

Through it all, US domestic spending and growth have remained resilient — ​good ​news from one perspective, but an additional inflation challenge for the Fed.

"We have both strong demand forces and ​supply forces working themselves through the economy," Musalem said.

When your phone drops one network and connects to another, the VPN may need to re-establish that tunnel. Usually, this happens so quickly that you barely notice. However, a weak signal, slow hotel login page or network that takes a few extra seconds to connect can create a brief period when your device has internet access before the VPN reconnects. This can happen during completely ordinary activities. You might switch from cellular data to airport Wi-Fi after landing. Later, your phone may move from the airport network to your hotel's Wi-Fi. The same thing can happen when your phone wakes from sleep in a new location or reconnects after losing cellular service. For travelers who move between networks frequently, those transitions are worth paying attention to. What happens when your VPN is disconnected When your VPN is disconnected, websites and online services can generally see the public IP address assigned by your internet provider or Wi-Fi network instead of the VPN server's IP address. That address can reveal information such as your approximate location and internet provider. A VPN also helps prevent the operator of a Wi-Fi network from easily seeing details about the internet services your device is contacting. Most trusted websites and apps already encrypt sensitive traffic using HTTPS or other encryption. That greatly reduces what someone monitoring a public Wi-Fi connection can see. However, risks remain if you connect to a fake or compromised Wi-Fi network. Someone controlling the network may try to direct you to a fraudulent login page, interfere with your connection or exploit websites and apps that are not properly encrypted. A VPN adds another layer of protection by encrypting traffic between your device and the VPN server and masking your normal public IP address. A kill switch can provide an additional safeguard by preventing internet traffic from leaving your device if the VPN unexpectedly disconnects. 1) Turn on VPN auto-connect The first setting to check is auto-connect. Most VPN apps offer some form of automatic connection. Without it, your VPN may stay disconnected until you remember to open the app and turn it back on. After a long flight, a trip through baggage claim and the rush to reach your hotel, that can be easy to forget. With auto-connect enabled, your VPN can attempt to restore its connection automatically when your device gets back online or joins a new network. Check your VPN app before traveling and make sure its automatic connection options are configured the way you want them. THE TRICK TO SMOOTHER STREAMING AT HOME AND ON THE ROAD 2) Enable your VPN kill switch The second setting to check is the kill switch. A VPN kill switch is designed to block internet traffic if your VPN unexpectedly disconnects. That helps prevent your device from simply falling back to an unprotected connection while the VPN is trying to reconnect. However, kill switches do not all work exactly the same way. Some protect you only when the VPN connection unexpectedly drops. Others can be configured to block internet access whenever the VPN is not connected. Android users may also have system-level options such as Always-on VPN and Block connections without VPN, depending on their device and VPN provider. Some reputable VPN services also offer additional kill switch options on supported platforms. Keep in mind that stronger settings that block all traffic outside the VPN can interfere with local network features or internet access when the VPN is intentionally turned off. The important thing is to understand how your VPN's kill switch works before you depend on it while traveling. Watch for airport and hotel Wi-Fi login pages There is one situation that can complicate things: the captive portal. That's the webpage airports, hotels and other public Wi-Fi networks sometimes require you to open before they grant internet access. You may need to accept terms, enter a room number or complete another login step. Because your device does not yet have normal internet access, the VPN may not be able to connect until you finish that process. Strict kill switch settings can occasionally make this more difficult. If you encounter a Wi-Fi login page, complete the network's sign-in process and then confirm that your VPN is connected before opening email, financial accounts or other sensitive services. Also make sure you are joining the correct Wi-Fi network. If you are uncertain, ask an airport employee, hotel staff member or business employee for the official network name. 3) Choose a VPN protocol that reconnects quickly Settings help, but reconnection speed also depends on the underlying technology your VPN uses. This is known as the VPN protocol. Different VPN protocols handle network changes in different ways. Some are particularly well suited to phones and laptops that frequently move between Wi-Fi and cellular connections. WHY YOUR VPN KEEPS GETTING BLOCKED AND THE SIMPLE FIX A quick VPN checklist for travelers Before your next trip, take a minute to check your VPN: You should also test your setup before leaving home. Connect to your VPN, turn Wi-Fi off and switch to cellular data. Then turn Wi-Fi back on and watch what your VPN does. Does it reconnect automatically? Does the kill switch block traffic while the VPN is disconnected? How long does the connection take to return? A quick test can help you catch a setting that needs attention before you are relying on your VPN in an airport or hotel. Kurt's key takeaways Most websites already use HTTPS encryption, so a brief VPN interruption does not leave all of your online activity exposed. Still, a VPN provides another valuable layer of privacy when you are using networks you do not control. The biggest issue for travelers is making sure the VPN actually reconnects when a phone or laptop moves between cellular service, airport Wi-Fi, hotel Wi-Fi and other networks. Turn on auto-connect, understand how your kill switch works and use a protocol that handles network changes efficiently. A few minutes spent checking your settings before a trip can help keep your VPN connection more consistent while you are on the move. articles.title: White House drafting executive order to take over NIH grant approvals: Reports
articles.summary: The Trump administration is reportedly putting together an executive order to move the National Institutes of Health’s (NIH) grant approval process away from the agency and giving political appointees more control. Reports emerged over the weekend that the Oval Office was considering enforcing more political oversight into NIH’s grantmaking process. The Washington Post was first…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is reportedly putting together an executive order to move the National Institutes of Health’s (NIH) grant approval process away from the agency and giving political appointees more control.

Reports emerged over the weekend that the Oval Office was considering enforcing more political oversight into NIH’s grantmaking process.

The Washington Post was first to report of a fraught meeting held in the Oval Office on Friday in which senior administration staffers argued over whether NIH was continuing to fund research at odds with President Trump’s priorities.

White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought reportedly accused NIH of funding “woke” initiatives. NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya reportedly defended his agency’s grantmaking process.

The New York Times reported on Sunday that the administration had begun drafting an executive order to create an external committee that would have the power to veto awards that don’t align with Trump’s political agenda. NIH spokesperson Joshua Pradko told the outlet that no NIH funds would be rescinded.

When reached for comment, Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) senior press secretary Emily Hilliard said in a statement to The Hill: “HHS remains focused on NIH’s core mission of supporting rigorous biomedical research that improves the health of the American people. We will continue to prioritize Gold Standard Science, transparency, and responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars.”

NIH funding has been ensnared in political crosshairs since the start of the second Trump administration. In June, the administration quietly rolled out a proposed rule that would de-emphasize peer review and give wide latitude to political appointees to decide what research will “advance the President’s policy priorities.”

Earlier this month, Democrats claimed the Pentagon had sought to divert NIH biomedical research funds to defense spending. HHS said at the time that the two agencies were exploring “potential avenues of collaboration.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House and OMB for comment.

articles.title: Duffy: A ‘human’ will always be in charge of AI air traffic program
articles.summary: “It’s always going to be a human that manages the airspace in America,” Duffy said.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy sought to assure Americans on Monday that a “human” will always manage U.S. airspace while unveiling a new AI tool aimed at helping air traffic controllers manage congestion and reduce flight delays.

“It’s always going to be a human that manages the airspace in America,” Duffy said during the event in Washington.

The Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories , or SMART, program will use AI to analyze air travel, airport capacity and weather. The rollout will begin at Reagan Washington National (DCA), Dulles International (IAD) and Baltimore-Washington International (BWI) airports, according to the Transportation Department (DOT).

“This tool won’t manage the airspace, but it gives us better information, better data to manage the airspace on behalf of the American people,” the DOT chief added.

Officials have worked to calm AI fears in recent days after several Anthropic researchers raised concerns about the potential for artificial intelligence to become uncontrollable — with one warning AI could potentially destroy humanity by the end of the decade.

That prompted calls for policymakers and regulators to take the warnings seriously , even as the exact risks remain difficult to measure or independently verify.

President Trump, however, has lashed out against concerns about rogue AI , claiming that any efforts to limit the technology are part of a “SICK conspiracy.”

“AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX,” Trump posted on social media.

Duffy said Monday the SMART program shows America continues to lead in aviation technology.

“(SMART) is going to help us provide a different experience for the American people,” he said. “I want to be clear again: This has not been deployed anywhere in the world; America was the first in flight.”

“We’re the ones that helped the world set up air traffic control, and we are again leading the world in new technology to bring more efficiency and a better experience to the American people,” the secretary added.

articles.title: Frightening object caught by TSA inside passenger's baseball bat-shaped flashlight
articles.summary: A concealed knife hidden inside a baseball bat-shaped flashlight was found sewn into a bag's lining at Tampa International Airport in Florida by TSA officers. An expert shares analysis.
articles.body: A passenger's attempt to bring an unusual item through airport security in Florida quickly caught the attention of highly trained Transportation Security Administration (TSA) officers. At Tampa International Airport recently, TSA officers discovered a 4-inch, double-edged knife concealed inside a baseball bat-shaped flashlight, according to an employee story published on the agency's website. TSA Officer Andrew Carter was screening the passenger's carry-on bag with an X-ray machine when he noticed something unusual about the flashlight — and flagged the bag for a closer look. TSA OFFICER SEES ALARMING SHAPES ON X-RAY BEFORE STOLEN CIVIL WAR MYSTERY UNRAVELS "The makeup and composition of the flashlight appeared unusual and outside what I typically expect, so I determined it required further examination," Carter said in the published note. Supervisory TSA Officer Michael Slaughter then searched the bag — and felt a mass beneath its lining. After opening the lining, he found the baseball bat-shaped flashlight and noticed a line along its shaft. "That is when it detached from the flashlight — revealing a 4-inch double-edged knife integrated into the handle," he said. When the passenger was questioned, he initially said he did not know the item was in his bag. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER But after airport police arrived, he said he'd placed it beneath the suitcase lining to save space, according to TSA. The passenger was arrested and was not allowed to travel, the agency said. Keith Jeffries, the Florida-based vice president of K2 Security Screening Group and a former federal security director for TSA at Los Angeles International Airport, told Fox News Digital that concealed blades are not unheard of at airport checkpoints. "It's not uncommon to see artfully concealed blades inside of items," Jeffries said. He pointed to walking canes as one example, noting that passengers are sometimes unaware that a blade is inside an item they purchased. "Once you do that, that falls right into the category of artful concealment — which leads to certainly a grave concern," he said. Passengers who bring knives to checkpoints may be able to voluntarily surrender them and continue traveling, while law enforcement decisions depend on the circumstances of each incident, TSA said. articles.title: FAA rolls out air traffic AI tool in Washington region
articles.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the Department of Transportation launched a new artificial intelligence tool in the Washington, D.C., area Monday intended to predict flight delays and advise air traffic controllers. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a press conference that the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routing and Trajectories (SMART) tool is the most…
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the Department of Transportation launched a new artificial intelligence tool in the Washington, D.C., area Monday intended to predict flight delays and advise air traffic controllers.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a press conference that the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routing and Trajectories (SMART) tool is the most advanced air traffic management system in the world and is being deployed for the first time in the D.C. area.

Duffy added that the tool — which cost the department $875 million — will ingest real-time flight data as well as current and future weather conditions to recommend necessary flight path changes to air traffic controllers.

“Humans sometimes don’t always make the right decisions,” he said. “Our system actually takes all of that data and gives a prompt to a human on how to better manage the airspace.”

Duffy stressed that human controllers will always manage American airspace. He said the SMART tool will advise the controllers with better information and data on the current and future conditions.

SMART allows controllers to have a real-time view of which planes are at the gate, taxiing and waiting for departure. It provides controllers with information on how long a plane has been waiting to take off by changing the color of the plane on the analyst’s screen, giving controllers visual cues on the status of departing flights.

Duffy said SMART will create a better flight experience for the American people by making American airspace more efficient.

“This is what America asked for,” Duffy said. “They said, ‘I’m sick of the experience that I have right now in America, I’m sick of the delays.’”

Bryan Bedford, administrator of the FAA, clarified that SMART will not be used by controllers whose job it is to prevent collisions and maintain safety — 15,000 of whom operate at airports across the country.

Instead, the tool will be used by traffic analysts who use data to decide whether to close or open certain airspace through ground stops and similar procedures.

Bedford said the FAA’s current procedure is to open or close airspace based on at-ground weather conditions, not the conditions at flight altitude. He added that SMART can show how a storm may shift in the near future and will allow personnel to factor in accurate weather data and predicted patterns to make flying more efficient.

“We think we can use better predictive analytics and we can use the better understanding of how weather is evolving and its intensity at altitude, and we can make much better airspace decisions,” Bedford said.

Bedford then demonstrated how the SMART system helps controllers view when two or more flights are set to land at a conflicting time. The new technology allows them to direct the flights and tweak flight paths or speeds so all flights can land without severe delays.

Duffy said SMART has been deployed in the D.C. region — at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Dulles International Airport and Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport — and will be expanded to other areas in the future. He said SMART serves as an update to decades-old technology currently used across the country.

“What we’ve thought through is, let’s use the best technology possible, the best predictors possible so humans can make the best decisions possible,” Duffy said. “And when we make the best decisions possible that means you have less delays and you have less cancellations.”

Duffy repeatedly stressed that humans will continue to control airspace and said there will be a gradual improvement to the flying experience as Americans continue to fly.

“The future of aviation is months away as we deploy these new tools,” the secretary said.

articles.title: Diesel is over $6 in 49 states: Where prices are highest and lowest
articles.summary: California has the most expensive diesel in the U.S. at an average of $8.42 per gallon, according to AAA.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Diesel hit a fresh record of $6.51 per gallon Monday, but prices in the most expensive state are nearly $2 higher.

In California, diesel costs an average of $8.42 per gallon, up from $5.16 a year ago, according to AAA data . Diesel was also over $7 in Washington and Hawaii to start the week.

The national average has risen nearly $1 over the past month amid the ongoing war in Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries . A year ago, diesel cost $3.70 per gallon, about $2.80 less than it is now.

Most Americans don’t drive diesel cars, but the fuel is the lifeblood of the freight sector, which means it’s gotten more expensive to transport nearly everything Americans buy at the store.

As of Monday, diesel is over $6 per gallon in 49 states, with Texas the lone exception at $5.97.

“Any broader directional change will depend heavily on overseas developments, and with new Houthi attacks and fresh U.S.-Iran escalations, the outlook remains deeply uncertain,” Patrick De Haan, GasBuddy’s head of petroleum analysis, wrote in a post Monday .

Which states have the highest diesel prices?

The five most expensive states are all out West, a region that’s relatively isolated from the nation’s main refining hubs and where fuel taxes tend to be higher.

That’s especially true in California, where taxes and fees add roughly $1.17 to every gallon of diesel, more than in any other state, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration .

Several Midwestern states, including Indiana, Michigan and Ohio, also have diesel prices above the national average after recording steep increases over the past week. Diesel is around $6.80 a gallon in all three, up more than 60 cents from a week earlier.

Which states have the lowest diesel prices?

Texas has the lowest diesel prices in the country at $5.97 per gallon, up from $3.19 a year ago.

Diesel is also below the national average, about $6 per gallon, in nearby Oklahoma, Louisiana and Mississippi.

Fuel prices tend to be lower near the Gulf Coast because that’s where much of the nation’s refining capacity is located. Those states generally have lower fuel taxes as well.

articles.title: Hegseth to chair Pentagon’s new homeland defense panel
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will now oversee a new Pentagon advisory committee focused on homeland security and defense — the first such department panel to do so. The Homeland Defense Board (HDB), announced in the Federal Register on Sept. 11 and first reported by Defense News, is meant to fill what the Pentagon sees as…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will now oversee a new Pentagon advisory committee focused on homeland security and defense — the first such department panel to do so.

The Homeland Defense Board (HDB), announced in the Federal Register on Sept. 11 and first reported by Defense News , is meant to fill what the Pentagon sees as a gap in the “specific, integrated advice” the Defense secretary needs to defend the homeland, which “is not available from any other Federal advisory committee, government agency, or alternative source,” according to the panel’s establishing documents.

“Over the past 10 years, rather than lessening, the threat from peer, near-peer, and rogue-state adversaries, in addition to non-state actors and hostile asymmetric activities, has become more intense and complex,” the justifying documents state.

As adversaries are actively projecting economic, cyber and military power into the Western Hemisphere, the new board will provide “critical, independent assessments” of the Defense Department’s “hemispheric defensive posture and domestic security preparedness.”

The documents argue that because other agencies and departments operate within specific mission or geographic areas, they are constrained or unsuited in advising on certain military issues.

The Department of Homeland Security’s advisory council, for example, “focuses exclusively on civilian law enforcement, border management, and emergency response” and “lacks the mandate to advise on Title 10 or Title 32 [domestic troop] deployments” and military-specific crises responses.

And the State Department’s International Security Advisory Board’s focus on diplomacy and arms control makes it “unequipped” to evaluate military campaign plans or defense strategies in North and South America.

The documents continue to state that relying solely on internal Defense Department “staff or contracted studies is also insufficient, as it fails to provide the consensus-based, independent, and external peer review required at the highest levels of strategic decision-making.”

The documents add that without the HDB, the Defense Department “risks strategic blind spots in its primary mission to protect the Homeland.”

The new board follows Hegseth’s purge of all members of existing Pentagon advisory panels in March 2025 after he ordered a 45-day “zero-based review” to determine if the roughly 40 such committees were aligned with the Trump administration’s policy priorities.

Completed in May the same year, the review proposed cutting 14 different defense advisory groups including the Defense Advisory Committee on Women in the Services, which was first established in 1951. Hegseth accused the committee of “ advancing a divisive feminist agenda ,” before terminating it.

According to the establishing documents, the HDB will be made up of 20 members “who are eminent authorities” in the fields of homeland defense, military strategy, defense support of civil authorities, interagency integration, critical infrastructure and cybersecurity, strategic competition, and western hemisphere policy.

The members will include Hegseth as chair; the Defense Department’s assistant secretary for Homeland Defense and Americas Security Affairs as vice chair; and one Pentagon civilian officer and one field-grade or mid-grade officer from each military department, among others.

The new board comes amid an ongoing military campaign at the U.S.-Mexico border; strikes on suspected drug carrying boats around Central and South America; and a large-scale deployment of the National Guard to U.S. cities, including more than 3,000 troops in Washington, D.C., in support of law enforcement.

There also are growing fears that President Trump could deploy federalized National Guard troops around polling locations ahead of the November midterm elections or seek to use the military to influence elections, even as federal laws prevent such action, NPR reported last week .

GOP nominees call for end to Iran war while on campaign trail

The Republican Senate candidates in Iowa and Michigan on Monday both called for an end to the U.S. war in Iran , citing the rising fuel costs for those in their respective states.

Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), vented voters’ frustrations by declaring that Iowans “ shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran.”

And former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), in a campaign ad said “ Michigan families can’t afford to wait ” for the Iran war to reach its conclusion, calling for an end to the conflict.

Hinson’s and Roger’s decision to link the seven-month military conflict to rising prices in the United States is a notable acknowledgment by a GOP candidate in a key battleground state where President Trump’s foreign policy is hitting Americans hard in the wallet.

Hinson called for suspending the gas tax, pausing diesel exports, loosening restrictions on gas with higher blends of ethanol and instituting a “diesel relief program to help our farmers and truckers being crushed by high costs .”

“These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end . I am working every day to deliver bipartisan results for Iowans and I will work with anyone who is ready to tackle this challenge immediately,” she wrote.

Rogers, meanwhile, released a campaign ad on X showing him at a grocery store. He said that Michiganders are struggling with rising prices as a result of the conflict and that prices must go down .

“The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly ,” he continued. “When it does, energy costs will plummet. But Michigan families can’t afford to wait for that to happen. We need to do something now.”

Rogers proposed suspending the state and federal gas tax of 70 cents a gallon and called for a temporary embargo on American diesel exports until the conflict is over. An increase in supply going to farmers and truckers will put “downward pressure” on the price of diesel.

Iran’s effective shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world’s oil is exported, has led to sharply rising gas and diesel prices.
